questions: Did the difficulty walking begin suddenly, within the last few days?
Do you have weakness on one side of your body?
Do you have numbness or loss of sensation in either leg?
Do you have pain in your hip, knee, or ankle when walking?
Have you recently had a stroke or other brain injury?
Do you feel dizzy or unsteady even when standing still?
Have you had difficulty walking like this for more than six months?
Do your legs feel weak when you try to walk?
Can you walk normally without using a walking aid?
Do you use the walking aid mainly because you are afraid of falling?
Do you have trouble lifting either foot off the ground?
Do you have stiffness or slowness of movement in both legs?
Have you had problems with balance or walking before this current hospital admission?
Did the walking problem begin after an operation or significant injury?
Does your walking difficulty vary markedly from one attempt to another?
Can you walk better when distracted or when you do not think about walking?
Do you ever suddenly collapse while remaining conscious, without actually injuring yourself?
Have doctors previously diagnosed you with a neurological disease affecting movement?
Do you have episodes of shaking, jerking, or abnormal posturing of your legs?
Do you have urinary urgency or episodes of urinary incontinence?
Have you or your family noticed a decline in your memory or thinking?
Do you take medication for Parkinson’s disease or another movement disorder?
Do you have a tremor when your hands are at rest?
Do you take sedatives, sleeping tablets, or other medication that makes you drowsy or unsteady?
Have you consumed a large amount of alcohol regularly in the past year?
Have you been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease?
Do you take levodopa or carbidopa/levodopa (such as Sinemet or Madopar)?
Does your walking improve noticeably after taking that medication?
Do you take the medication because of slowness or stiffness rather than tremor?
Do you have episodes in which your feet feel stuck to the floor when you try to start walking or turn?
Have you had repeated falls since the walking problem began?
Do you have slowness of movement in your arms or hands?
Do you have stiffness in your arms or legs on examination?
Do you have difficulty looking up or down, especially looking downward?
Have you been taking an antipsychotic drug or metoclopramide (such as haloperidol, risperidone, or domperidone) regularly?
Do you have a history of multiple small strokes, high blood pressure, diabetes, or other vascular disease?
Was levodopa prescribed mainly for restless legs or uncomfortable sensations in your legs?
Has your walking progressively worsened over weeks to a few months?
Have you developed memory or thinking problems since the walking difficulty began?
Have you had sudden, brief jerks of your arms, legs, or body (myoclonus)?
Have you developed visual symptoms, slurred speech, or difficulty swallowing?
Have you developed poor coordination or difficulty using your hands?
Did the symptoms begin within the past year?
orders: Bedside neurological examination including assessment of strength, tone, reflexes, plantar responses, coordination, proprioception, and sensory testing in all limbs.
Observe the patient walking without assistance, including initiation, turning, stepping over an obstacle, tandem gait, and walking backward.
Perform the retropulsion (pull) test and assess for freezing of gait.

MRI of the brain without contrast, including T1, T2/FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, susceptibility-weighted, and mid-sagittal sequences, to assess for vascular parkinsonism, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, structural lesions, and midbrain atrophy.

Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal-fluid real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assay for prion disease, CSF 14-3-3 and total tau levels, cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, and infectious studies.
Electroencephalography (EEG) to assess for periodic sharp-wave complexes and other encephalopathic abnormalities.
Ask the patient’s family about rapidly progressive cognitive decline, myoclonus, visual or cerebellar symptoms, and the exact time course of progression.
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
gait observation including turning and doorways
MRI brain - midbrain (hummingbird sign, midbrain-to-pons ratio)
MRI brain - white matter and ventricles (small-vessel disease, ventriculomegaly)
CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
lumbar puncture / CSF (cells, protein, Abeta42/40, total tau, p-tau)
